Comprendre les non-dits du consentement: Understanding the Unspoken Side of Consent
De façon plus ou moins automatique, quan: Almost automatically, when we say consent, we think of sex.
<em>Cet article sur le consentement comp: This article on consent has two parts. The first, “Consent: How to Apply It in Everyday Life?”, looks at what consent is, while the second deals with how to apply it in everyday life.
De façon plus ou moins automatique, quan: Almost automatically, when we say consent, we think of sex. We think of slogans like “No means no” or “Sans oui, c’est non” (“Without a yes, it’s a no”). We remember the revelations sparked by the #MeToo movement, along with the debates on sexual and domestic violence. But this issue goes beyond “yes,” “no” or sex.
Le consentement ne concerne pas seulemen: Consent doesn’t concern only survivors and perpetrators. It is everywhere: in the small decisions of daily life and in every relationship, whether family, friendship, romantic or professional. It is precisely because it affects everyone that it is harder to put into practice in everyday life. Many challenges make consent difficult to apply, to live and to share.
Parmi ces défis, il y a la pression soci: Among these challenges is social pressure, which Annick* knows well. A teacher of French to adults at the Centre de services scolaire de Montréal (CSSDM), the young woman has a free, open and honest view of relationships. She tends to describe herself as a libertine. She tells us about an evening when she turned down a man’s advances. “I went to have dinner at a couple’s place. At one point, she went to bed and I stayed with him. He tried to kiss me, but I said no.
Selon mes amis, j’aurais dû partir quand: “According to my friends, I should have left when she went to bed, I should have felt the tension between him and me,” she says, wondering what she did wrong. “But I felt like I’d made a big step forward, because I said no and I stuck to it!”
Elle explique qu’elle continue à accepte: She explains that she still agrees to things she later regrets, or consents to sex she doesn’t really want, because it’s what the other person expects of her. “It’s hard to date someone without them expecting that we’ll sleep together,” she says.
Annick a donc l’impression d’accepter su: Annick feels she mostly says yes so as not to disappoint, to meet the expectations people have of her, and believes these various pressures influence her choices or make them confusing. “When you’re a woman, you’re under strong pressures that affect your decisions,” she laments.
« Ce n’est pas uniquement aux hommes de: “It’s not only up to men to question themselves. Socialization is still binary, patriarchal and sexist. We’re raised in these problematic dynamics: women who know what they want are frightening, and it’s up to the man to be strong and to ‘make a move,’” explains Nesrine Bessaih, an anthropologist and, with the collective La CORPS féministe, co-author of Corps accord : guide de sexualité positive. So that consent isn’t just a theory people study, she would like to see the issue of consent popularized.
Le consentement commence dès l’enfance,: Consent begins in childhood, and its absence can lead to sexual violence as early as the <l1>schoolyard</l1>. While the mandatory sex education classes introduced in 2018 are encouraging because of their more positive and diverse approach, Kharoll-Ann Souffrant, a social worker and doctoral student in social work, finds them insufficient. In her view, filling these gaps means that the notion of consent must not be addressed only in sexual terms, but also extended to everyday life.
« Il faudrait développer la capacité des: “We should develop young people’s ability to say they’re not comfortable, as well as their sensitivity and their listening to others,” she explains, adding that consent has to become a concrete reality before it is taught. That is what Valérie and François are trying to do with their children. “I want my girls, like my boys, to get into the habit of asking and to feel free to give their consent – and to do so in an informed way,” says Valérie.
« Si on fait une sortie, je reste démocr: “If we go on an outing, I stay democratic. I listen to their ideas, even though I always keep a right of veto as a parent,” continues François. Valérie and François have been together for seven years.
Âgés de 39 et 40 ans, ils sont chacun le: Aged 39 and 40, they each have two children and had a daughter together. They live in Joliette and, in their relationship as in their family, consent is everywhere. They talk a lot and regularly review the rules of their life together and their limits. “We’re always changing, so something that used to be acceptable to me can stop being so, and vice versa.”
Loin d’être irréprochables, ils peuvent: Far from perfect, they can also hit roadblocks. “Sometimes I can be uncomfortable and unable to express myself logically. It can take me up to a few days to think before I talk to François about it,” says Valérie.
François ajoute qu’il fait constamment a: François adds that he is constantly careful because, even after years together, he is still afraid of causing harm. Like other men, he fears crossing Valérie’s boundaries without knowing it, even when she agrees. Because consent isn’t only verbal. It is also expressed physically, through gestures and attitude – in short, through non-verbal language, which makes up 90% of communication.
Une proposition ne nous plaît pas ? On c: Don’t like a proposal? We cross our arms, step back, our voice gets lower, but we end up agreeing so as not to hurt the other person, because it’s not that big a deal, or because the other person is really enthusiastic.
Être à l’écoute du non verbal n’est pas: Being attuned to non-verbal cues isn’t always easy, so much so that it can be useful to ask for verbal confirmation. That is the approach François favours when he isn’t sure.
« J’essaie toujours d’obtenir un consent: “I always try to get explicit consent by asking a lot of questions and reassuring her as much as possible so that she feels comfortable telling me no,” he explains. Indeed, just because his partner says “yes” doesn’t necessarily mean she is fully on board. To be valid, consent must be free, informed and enthusiastic. “Enthusiastic” because the person consenting must know themselves, know what they like and don’t like, and understand their desires.
Le mode de vie de Valérie et de François: Valérie and François’s way of life is proof that consent can be applied in everyday life and in all relationships. However, their approach demands a great deal of self-examination. We all remember a situation where we may have consented without really wanting to, moments when we acted without paying attention to the fact that the other person wasn’t fully enthusiastic. But who has ever thought about it more deeply, going beyond the couple or the sexual relationship, in order to change how they think and act?
Jordan* est un graphiste de 39 ans. Céli: Jordan* is a 39-year-old graphic designer. Recently single, he lives alone in a studio apartment in Montréal.
Notre discussion l’amène à réfléchir au: Our conversation leads him to reflect on consent and on his relationships. He says he has changed a lot with age. When he was younger, he paid less attention to the consent of the women he dated, not out of abuse, but out of carelessness and thoughtlessness. Jordan also explains that, like many others, he has sometimes forced himself, consenting without desire to his partner’s wishes. “As a man, there’s the fact that you don’t want to come across as bad in bed, that you want to satisfy the other person,” he reflects. His story echoes that of many others.
Il peut être parfois difficile de bien c: It can sometimes be hard to properly understand what you want or to know how to express it. That’s because consent involves two steps: understanding your own desires, needs and discomforts, but also knowing how to share them with the other person. For some, developing self-awareness is a major challenge.
Ce peut être le cas de ceux qui font pas: This may be the case for those who put other people’s happiness before their own, or for those so ruled by routine that they no longer listen to their bodies. For others, communication is the problem.
Dire non à l’autre peut l’offenser ou le: Saying no to someone can offend or disappoint them. And there is also the risk of revealing a sensitivity or vulnerability that we weren’t raised to show. So how do we get to know ourselves and express ourselves?
